newsitem.title: FRANCE: French court to rule on war crimes trial for Papon.
newsitem.headline: French court to rule on war crimes trial for Papon.

text.p: The French Supreme Court will rule on Thursday on whether a former cabinet minister should stand trial for crimes against humanity, probably the last chance to put collaboration with the Nazis in the dock.
The court's decision will be a decisive step in a 15-year judicial marathon in which career civil servant Maurice Papon, 87, benefited from delaying tactics by successive governments.

In a last-ditch attempt to avoid trial for World War Two crimes, Papon had appealed to the supreme court after an appeals court in Bordeaux ruled last September that he should stand trial for sending 1,690 Jews including 223 children to Nazi death camps in 1942-44.
Public prosecutors have built up a dossier of 50,000 pages against Papon, who was secretary-general of the Bordeaux administration in the collaborationist Vichy government.
He would be only the second Frenchman -- and probably the last -- to be sent to trial on such charges arising from the war.

A lower-ranking collaborationist, former militia officer Paul Touvier, was jailed for life in 1994 and died in prison last year aged 81. Another accused collaborationist, Rene Bousquet, was shot dead by a publicity-hungry failed writer in 1993 before he could stand trial.
The Bordeaux appeals court sent Papon to a jury trial in an assize court on charges of being an accomplice to the kidnapping and murder of deportees eventually sent to Nazi death camps.
The court also approved charges that Papon was an accomplice to arbitrary arrests, the arrest of minors under 15 years old, inhuman acts and attempted illegal arrests.

"Papon was the archetype of the opportunistic bureaucrat who wanted power at any price and who got it, who followed orders even when they were inhuman," argues lawyer Gerard Boulanger, who campaigned for victims' families for the past 15 years.

"This would be the first trial of a high civil servant focussing on the complicity of the French state in the Holocaust. There were large-scale purges after the war but they did not centre on the Holocaust," he said.

Prosecutors say the Holocaust was "one of the war's best-kept secrets" and that they have not managed to establish whether Papon knew the fate of the Jews he sent to Drancy in Paris, a transit camp for deportees to Nazi death camps.

Papon says he helped the Resistance, saved several Jews and watered down the harshest provisions taken by the Vichy government. His wartime record unknown, he enjoyed a meteoric post-war career, serving as Paris police chief in 1958-67 and budget minister in 1978-81.

But in 1981, wartime arrest warrants, chartering of trains and other orders bearing Papon's signature were found. Legal proceedings began in 1983 but were annulled on technicalities in 1987, started again from scratch and were finally completed in June 1995.
The late President Francois Mitterrand, himself a former Vichy official, sought to prevent trials for crimes against humanity because he said they undermined national unity.
His Gaullist successor Jacques Chirac acknowledged in 1995 French state responsibility in the deportation of the Jews, the first post-war leader to do so.
